report:
Short answer
Model B (relative to A) injects a strong “news/blog/social‑media/ads/celebrity” style signal at the start of sequences — i.e., the difference drives vocabulary associated with blogs, media, ads and public‑figure/news tokens and so would bias early continuations toward that domain.

Why I think that
- The L2‑norm of the difference is concentrated in early token positions (p0–p2) and especially in middle→late layers (layers ~16–25). That pattern indicates a change that will strongly affect next‑token selection early in generation.
- The logit‑lens top tokens for the highest‑norm cells are coherently themed across layers and positions: frequent hits include blog/blogger/blogging, facebook, photo/video/film, ad/ads/TV/Mail, seminar/seminars/HDTV, metropolitan/chairman/spokesman, Obama/politicians/journalists, billionaire/money. Many layers repeatedly point to “blogs / blogger / blogging / blog” and to advertising/media tokens.
- Position 1 cells often point to tokens like “ad”, “Mail”, “May”, “TV”, “-”, “(” which are characteristic of headlines/advert placements or metadata in scraped web/news content; positions 2–4 point strongly to blog/photo/video content words. The repetition across layers/positions strengthens the interpretation that this is a domain signal rather than isolated token noise.

Caveats / uncertainty
- I can’t say exactly why the models differ (e.g., different web‑data mixture, an advertising/news fine‑tune, or tokenization/training frequency shifts). The evidence supports a domain/style shift but not a specific training objective.
- Patchscope continuations would help confirm how this vector affects produced text in context; those readouts aren’t shown here.

Conclusion
The evidence supports naming a domain/style difference: Model B upweights a “web/news/blog/social‑media/advertising/celebrity” token cluster early in the residual stream, so B would be expected to bias early continuations toward bloggy/media/advertising language compared to A.
